To behold something means to see it — but not in a casual, everyday way. When you behold something, you are seeing it with your full attention, often with a feeling of wonder, awe, or deep admiration. It carries the sense that what you are looking at is striking, remarkable, or worthy of special notice.

Think of it this way: you see a bird fly past your window without much thought. But if a magnificent eagle spreads its wings right in front of you and you stop, stare, and feel a sense of amazement — that is beholding.

So the word packs two things together:

  • The act of seeing or looking
  • The emotional weight of that seeing — a sense that what you are witnessing matters, impresses, or moves you

"Behold" is a transitive verb, which means it always takes an object — there is always something being beheld.

  • She beheld the vast ocean for the first time.
  • He beheld his newborn daughter and wept with joy.
  • The crowd beheld the king as he entered the hall.

You behold something. The word doesn't work without a subject (the one seeing) and an object (the thing being seen).
The Word Feels Formal and Elevated

You will almost never hear someone use "behold" in ordinary conversation. If a friend calls you to the window to look at a stray cat, they'll say "Hey, look at this!" — not "Come, behold this!"

"Behold" belongs to a higher, more formal, literary, or ceremonial register. You find it in:

  • Religious and sacred texts (the Bible uses it constantly: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive...")
  • Classic literature and poetry
  • Speeches, proclamations, and ceremonies
  • Fantasy, mythology, and epic storytelling

When a writer or speaker chooses this word over "see" or "look," they are deliberately signaling that this moment is solemn, grand, or significant. The word itself adds drama and weight to whatever follows it.

One of the most common ways you will encounter "behold" is as a command — telling someone to look, pay attention, and appreciate what is in front of them.

  • "Behold the power of nature!"
  • "Behold — the treasure you have sought for so long!"
  • "Behold the work of a thousand craftsmen!"

In this usage, the speaker is not just saying "look over there." They are saying: "Stop. Pay full attention. What you are about to see deserves your complete focus and wonder." It is a call to witness something meaningful.

An important subtlety: beholding is not passive. You can see something without meaning to — light enters your eyes and you register an image. But to behold is to consciously, deliberately take in what is before you. It implies presence and awareness.

If someone says "She beheld the ruins of her childhood home," the sentence tells you she wasn't just glancing at it. She was standing there, fully aware of what she was seeing, taking it in with all its emotional meaning.
"Lo and Behold" — A Common Set Phrase

You will frequently encounter the expression "lo and behold," which is used to introduce something surprising or unexpected — often with a touch of humor or irony.

  • I searched everywhere for my keys, and lo and behold, they were in my coat pocket the whole time.
  • We thought the project was ruined, and lo and behold, it turned into our biggest success.

Here, "lo" is an old word also meaning "look" or "see," so "lo and behold" essentially means "look and see!" — drawing attention to something surprising that has just happened or been discovered. In modern usage, this phrase is very common and not considered archaic at all, unlike "behold" alone.

The noun form of this verb is beholder — simply the person who beholds something.

You've likely heard the famous saying: "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder." This means that what one person finds beautiful, another may not — beauty is subjective and depends entirely on who is looking.

SituationUse "behold"?

Use "behold" when you want to convey that someone is seeing something remarkable with full awareness and often with awe. It is the right word when the act of seeing carries emotional, spiritual, or dramatic significance. It is almost always used in formal, literary, religious, or elevated contexts — not in everyday speech.

When you read or hear it, it is a signal: what is being seen here is not ordinary. Pay attention.

• Standing at the edge of the canyon, she beheld a landscape unlike anything she had ever seen.
  • The shepherd boys beheld a star that burned brighter than all the rest.
  • "Behold what courage looks like," the general said, pointing to the soldier.
  • He opened the vault and beheld, for the first time, the painting that had been lost for centuries.
  • Lo and behold, after years of searching, the answer had been in the first chapter all along.

In short: to behold is to truly see — with your eyes open, your mind present, and your heart moved.
